description: Solo high school junior experienced with engineering, AI development, and data science. Working towards developing a novel approach for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator Challenge.
summary:
Lunar Plan B is an interactive mission planner that shows what happens when a lunar south pole landing is delayed. Users can change the landing site and touchdown time, see when ridges block sunlight or the line of sight to Earth, and test whether a revised schedule can still return the mission’s science data.

The app combines NASA/JPL Horizons observations with NASA LRO/LOLA elevation data to calculate when a lander can generate power or communicate. In our featured de Gerlache Rim scenario, a 24-hour landing delay leaves only 30 usable minutes in a planned 90-minute transmission. Moving the transmission one hour earlier restores the full window in the simulation.

Lunar Plan B helps mission teams spot a risk that site averages can hide: a landing site may have hours of Earth visibility and still lose contact when a critical transmission is scheduled. By showing where the signal is blocked and testing a revised plan, the app helps teams explore recovery options before touchdown.
details:
Lunar Plan B helps mission teams see whether a lunar south pole landing plan can still deliver its science after touchdown slips. Users can change the landing site or touchdown time, see when terrain blocks the Sun or Earth, and compare the original schedule with a revised plan. The revised plan has to fit the available power and communication windows while respecting task order and deadlines.

At de Gerlache Rim, our featured scenario shows how a 24-hour delay leaves only 30 qualifying minutes in a planned 90-minute transmission. The simulator shows the ridge that blocks the lander’s line of sight to Earth. Moving the transmission one hour earlier restores the full modeled window. Users can also test the revised schedule at 16 points inside a landing ellipse to see whether it still works if the lander touches down away from its target.

The creative part is turning a terrain map into a tool for answering an operational question. A site can have plenty of sunlight and Earth visibility over an entire mission, yet still lose contact at the moment a critical transmission needs to happen. We built Lunar Plan B to help teams catch those timing conflicts early and compare recovery options before committing to a plan.

We used NASA/JPL Horizons for Sun and Earth positions, NASA LRO/LOLA elevation data for the terrain, and NASA SPICE for custom geometry. The app uses Python, FastAPI, and Google OR-Tools for analysis and scheduling, with a React and TypeScript interface hosted on Vercel. OpenAI Codex assisted with research, coding, and documentation. We considered terrain obstruction, sunlight, battery reserve, communication windows, task dependencies, and landing uncertainty. The spacecraft and mission assumptions are illustrative, so the results support early planning and exploration.
